attributes.title: Level 2

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Player sprite’s velocity y and acceleration y so it would jump when the A button is pressed, and then fall back to the ground?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓What happens when you change a sprite’s velocity y and acceleration y values?

❓Does the Player sprite jump and return to the ground as you expected?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they should make the Player sprite jump on the tilemap to check that it can reach each of the platforms. Encourage the ninja to think about the vy and ay values and if they feel like the right balance for the game.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to jump over, and on top of, Enemy sprites!


Add a [set sprite [x]] block underneath the Player sprite’s blocks in the [on start] container. Use the drop down to select [ay (acceleration y)]. Set the parameter to 600.


In the [on button pressed] container, replace the <true> value in the [if then] conditional with an <is sprite hitting wall> value block. Select [bottom] as the direction the program should check for. Then, add another [set sprite [x]] block into the conditional and select [vy (velocity y)] from the drop down. Set the parameter to -250.


Click ▶ to explore the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓Did you create a function, then call the function inside the [on start] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you create a new function?

❓ Where else do you think the [makeEnemy] function might be used in this project?

❓ Where will the Enemy sprites appear on the tilemap? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that functions can help organize their code and make it run more efficiently. Prompt the ninja to consider why a function might be useful in this example.
steps.instructions:
Use a function to create multiple Enemy sprites across the tilemap!


Create a new function named [makeEnemy]. Drag a [repeat] loop into the [function makeEnemy] container, and set the parameter to 12 to create 12 Enemy sprites. 


Drag the Enemy sprite’s blocks into the loop then replace those blocks in the [on start] container with a [call makeEnemy] block.


Use a (pick random) in the column parameter with the range 6 and 30, then set the row to 6 so Enemy sprites appear along the tilemap floor, but not too close to where the Player sprite starts!


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprites appear on the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use -60 to -30 as the vx range, so all Enemy sprites start off moving left, in the direction of the Player sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is the vx (velocity x) set to a range of negative numbers?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that negative x or vx values move a sprite to the left. Since the Player sprite is starting on the left side of the tilemap, the Enemy sprite should move in the direction of the Player at the start of the game.
steps.instructions:
Code the Enemy sprites to move across the tilemap!


Add a [set sprite [x]] block with [vx (velocity x)] selected in the [repeat] loop. Select the Enemy sprite name, then drag a (pick random) block into the parameter and set the range as -60 to -30.


Add a [set sprite bounce on wall] block, toggled <ON> so the Enemy sprites bounce on the tilemap walls.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprites move at different speeds across the tilemap floor!

steps.hints: ❓Did you select the correct dropdown directions inside the <is sprite hitting wall> blocks?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


﻿Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you drag a (value) variable into each of the <is sprite hitting wall> blocks?

❓ When will the Enemy sprite’s image change?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡As the ninja is building 2D platformer projects, it’s important that game design mechanics, such as the image of a sprite, match the perspective of the project. In this example, the Enemy sprite image is changed when it bounces on the wall and continues moving in the opposite direction.

💡Talk through why the [flip image horizontally] block will work on either left or right walls, and why the <or> operator is essential here. Guide ninjas to understand the difference between horizontal and vertical, if needed.

💡Make sure the Ninja uses the [on game update] loop, not the [on game update every ms] loop.
steps.instructions:
Code the Enemy sprites to face the direction they are moving in!


Drag out an [on game update] loop and add a [for element] loop with the (array of sprites of kind Enemy) as the (list). 


Drag an [if then] conditional into the [for element] loop. Open Logic to drag out an <or> block to replace <true>. 


From Scene, drag <is sprite hitting wall> blocks into both < > openings in the <or>. Use a (value) variable from the loop as the sprite name value, then select [left] for the first block and [right] for the other block.


From Images, under Advanced, drag a [flip picture horizontally] block into the conditional. From Sprites, drag out a (mySprite image) block to replace (picture) then replace (mySprite) with the (value) variable from the loop.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprites face the direction they are moving in!

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the two (mySprite x) bubbles to the correct sprites, and select [bottom] and [y] in the dropdown?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

﻿Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the < 0<0 > block check for? What condition needs to be true in order for the code inside the conditional to run?

❓What does the ((otherSprite) [y]) block tell you? Why is this useful?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Double check that the ninja has set the correct sprites and drop down selections in the < 0<0 > block and encourage them to test out jumping on top of sprites to destroy them.

💡 Walk through the logic of this example with the ninja. If the bottom of the Player sprite is less than the height of the Enemy sprite, destroy the Enemy sprite and reset the Player sprite’s velocity y.
steps.instructions:
Destroy Enemy sprites by jumping on top of them!


Drag an [if then] conditional into the [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container already in the code editor, and add a [destroy (otherSprite)] block inside. Replace <true> with a < 0<0 > block.


From Sprites, drag a (mySprite x) block into both parameters of the < 0<0 > block. On the left side, replace (mySprite) with the (sprite) bubble, then select [bottom] from the drop down. On the right side, replace (mySprite) with the (otherSprite) bubble, then select [y] from the drop down. Now, the Enemy sprite will only be destroyed if the bottom of the Player sprite overlaps it.


Code the Player sprite to “hop” up after jumping on an Enemy sprite by dragging a [set sprite x] block into the conditional, replacing (mySprite) with the (sprite) bubble, selecting [vy (velocity y)] from the drop down, and entering the parameter -100.


Create a new variable named [snakesStomped]. Set the variable to 0 in the [on start] container, and change the variable by 1 in the conditional inside the [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container.


Click ▶ to try jumping on Enemy sprites to destroy them!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add a [pause] block in between the two [set sprite ghost through sprites] blocks?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the project know if the the Player sprite is not successful at destroying an Enemy sprite?

❓ What does the [set sprite ghost through sprites] block do? How is it used in this example?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If the bottom of the Player sprite is not less than ((otherSprite) [y]), then the code in the [else] opening will run. If any other direction of the Player sprite overlaps the Enemy sprite, the code will not run.
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen if the Player sprite is not successful at destroying an Enemy sprite!


Inside the [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container, add an [else] opening to the conditional. Use [change score by] and [sprite start effect] blocks to make something happen when an Enemy sprite overlaps the Player sprite on any side other than the bottom.


To provide the Player sprite a 1-second recovery, drag 2 [set sprite auto destroy] blocks into the [else] opening. In both blocks, replace the sprite name with a (sprite) bubble and select [ghost through sprites] in the drop down. Toggle the first block to <ON>, and leave the second block <OFF>. Insert a [pause] block in between, and set the parameter to 1000ms.


Click ▶ to test what happens when an Enemy sprite overlaps a Player sprite.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the column and row ranges so the coins will appear above the platforms, away from the Enemy sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓Why might a function be helpful for placing Coin sprites on the tilemap?

❓Why should the Coin sprites be placed on the top half of the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The 2 Coin sprite blocks should already be in the starter code on the code editor. The ninja does not need to drag out new blocks.
steps.instructions:
Place Coin sprites across the tilemap for the Player sprite to collect!


Create a function named [makeCoin] then drag the coin sprite’s 2 blocks from [on start] into the function container. Use a [call makeCoin] block inside an [on game update every ms] loop that runs every 500ms.


Update the column (pick random) to 1 and 30 and update the row (pick random) to 1 and 3  so Coin sprites appear above the tilemap platforms, away from the Enemy sprites.


Then, drag in a [set sprite x] block to the function. Select the (coin) sprite name, [lifespan] from the drop down, and use a (pick random) in the parameter, with the range 2000 to 4000. This will make a coin sprite appear for 2-4 seconds in the upper part of the tilemap.


Click ▶ to see the tilemap fill with Coin sprites for the Player sprite to collect!

steps.hints: ❓Did you set both <0=0> blocks equal to the correct variables and values?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


﻿Ask the ninja:

❓ What condition(s) need to be true in order for the game to end in a win?

❓ Can either condition be true in order for the code in the conditional to run?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The <or> block checks to see if the first condition is true. If it is, then the code inside the conditional runs. If the first condition is false, then it checks to see if the second condition is true. If it is, then the code inside the conditional runs. Else, the code inside the conditional does not run.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to win by destroying 10 Enemy sprites or collecting 10 Coin sprites!


Drag out a [forever] loop and place an [if then] conditional inside, then place a [game over] block, toggled to <WIN>, inside the conditional. 


Open Logic to drag out an <or> block to replace <true>. Drag <0=0> blocks into both sides of the <or>, setting one side to check for the (score) = 10 and the other side to check for (snakesStomped) = 10. 


Click ▶ to test out winning the game by either collecting 10 Coin sprites or destroying 10 Enemy sprites!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add customizations to your project, such as dialog boxes, splash screens, or effects?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might help a user understand how to play the game?

❓ What sound effects might you add for each overlap event?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize the project by adding game directions with a dialog box, and sound effects when the Player sprite overlaps the Enemy and Coin sprites!


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a 2D platformer project where a Player sprite must either collect coins or jump on top of snakes to destroy them in order to win!

validationItems.text: Player sprite jumps up when the A button is pressed and the bottom of the sprite is touching a tilemap wall tile.
Create and position 12 Enemy sprites using a function.
Enemy sprites move at different speeds and bounce on tilemap walls.
Enemy sprites face the direction they are moving in.
Player sprite can destroy Enemy sprites by jumping on top of them.
Player sprite loses a point and  gets a 1 second recovery if it overlaps an Enemy sprite.
Coin sprites appear across the tilemap.
Game ends when Player sprite destroys 10 Enemy sprites OR collects 10 Coin sprites.
Game instructions are shared in a dialog box. Sound effects are added to the game.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 2 of Green Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about Booleans and logic operators. Booleans can be useful to check if specific and/or multiple conditions have been met in a project. They can also be useful in 2D platformer projects to keep track of certain game conditions and to make something happen on certain tilemap events. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 2:

badges.title: It All Keeps Adding Up
badges.description: Use logic and math to make different things happen in a project.

badges.title: All or Nothing
badges.description: Check if two conditions are both true in a conditional statement.

badges.title: Fork in the Road
badges.description: Check if one of two conditions is true in a conditional statement.

badges.title: Nuh-Uh!
badges.description: Check for the negative, or opposite, of a variable’s current value.

badges.title: Yes/No Question
badges.description: Set a condition using the Boolean values true or false.

badges.title: Knowing Your Surroundings
badges.description: Check for the tile next to a sprite before making something happen in a project.

badges.title: Splat!
badges.description: Set a sprite to be destroyed whenever it touches a tilemap wall.

badges.title: Math Magician
badges.description: Perform a mathematical operation in a project’s code.
